propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of five decisions dated October 21, 2024, rejecting the Principal Applicant's work permit application and dependents' applications.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of five decisions dated October 21, 2024, by an Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [IRCC] officer [the Officer], rejecting the work permit application of the first-named Applicant, Mohammad Umair [the Principal Applicant], under the International Mobility Program [the Program], as well as the applications of the other Applicants, his wife and children as accompanying dependents [the Dependents].

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of five decisions rejecting the Principal Applicant's and dependents' work permit applications.

propositions.text: This application for judicial review is dismissed because the Decision is reasonable and procedurally fair.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is dismissed, because the Decision (as defined later in these Reasons) is reasonable and procedurally fair.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review application, finding the Decision reasonable and procedurally fair.

propositions.text: The Applicants are Pakistani citizens; the Principal Applicant works in manufacturing and has an Ontario business producing lightweight building blocks.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are citizens of Pakistan. The Principal Applicant works in the manufacturing industry and has incorporated a business in Ontario, said to specialize in producing lightweight building blocks for construction.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicants are Pakistani citizens; the Principal Applicant works in manufacturing and has an Ontario business.

propositions.text: On June 4, 2024, the Principal Applicant applied for a one-year work permit under the Program; dependents also applied to join him.
propositions.quote: On June 4, 2024, the Principal Applicant submitted a work permit application under the Program for a period of one year. Applications were also submitted for the Dependents to join the Principal Applicant during his time in Canada.

propositions.text: The record includes supporting documents, including a Commitment Certificate from the Incubator dated December 4, 2023, expiring June 4, 2023.
propositions.quote: The record before the Court includes the documents submitted in support of those applications, including a Commitment Certificate issued by the so-called incubator under the Program [the Incubator], dated December 4, 2023, and expiring on June 4, 2023 [the Commitment Certificate].

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Principal Applicant applied for a one-year work permit on June 4, 2024, with dependents applying to join him, supported by documents including a Commitment Certificate.

propositions.text: On October 21, 2024, the Officer refused the applications and the Applicants filed for judicial review, which were consolidated by Justice McVeigh on December 19, 2024.
propositions.quote: On October 21, 2024, the Officer issued letters to each of the Applicants conveying the decision that their application had been refused. Each of the Applicants filled an application for leave and for judicial review of the decision refusing their application. By Order dated December 19, 2024, Justice McVeigh consolidated these applications under the present Court file number.

propositions.text: The court will refer to the refusals collectively as the “Decision”.
propositions.quote: For purposes of these Reasons, I will refer to the decisions on the Applicants’ applications collectively as the “Decision”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Officer refused the applications on October 21, 2024; judicial review applications were consolidated and collectively called the Decision.

propositions.text: The Officer was not satisfied the Principal Applicant would leave Canada as required by paragraph 179(b) IRPR, based on five listed grounds (a-e).
propositions.quote: The letter issued to the Principal Applicant stated that the Officer was not satisfied that he would leave Canada at the end of his stay as required by paragraph 179(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [IRPR], based on: (a) his current employment situation not showing that he was financially established in his country of residence; (b) the compensation indicated in his job offer and his assets and financial situation being insufficient to support the stated purpose of travel; (c) his inability to demonstrate that he would be able to adequately perform the work he sought; (d) his lack of significant family ties outside Canada; and (e) his inability to adequately demonstrate that he met the requirements of the work permit he sought under section 205 of the IRPR.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the Principal Applicant unlikely to leave Canada based on five specified grounds under paragraph 179(b) IRPR.

propositions.text: The Officer's GCMS notes detail concerns about financial documents, employment and education evidence, economic benefits, expired Commitment Certificate, and overall failure to meet A77 requirements.
propositions.quote: The following entry in the Officer’s Global Case Management System [GCMS] notes also informs an understanding of the reasons for the Decision: I have reviewed the application. Application under A77. Family of five. I note on the IMM 5766 that the applicant and one other person are listed as essential. Applicant's valuation/chartered account document(s) reviewed. These documents will not be considered given that the report(s) are a paid for document/statement and do not include evidence of funds available that have not already been reviewed. Funds available at time of application unclear due to dated bank statement in comparison to date of application. Bank statements for both the applicant and business partner are dated in 2023. Applicant’s stated employment and education noted however there is no supporting documentation to support this. As a result I am not satisfied the applicant that the applicant will be able to adequately perform the proposed work. Applicant’s representative describes economic benefits to include the hiring of “manufacturing, sales, administration and management” positions and the commitment certificate indicates one of the urgent business reasons to be to “hire a Canadian team” yet I note the financial forecast for salaries in the supplied deck notes salary costs to be under 50K CAD for each of the first 5 years of business. Applicant has not satisfied me of the creation of significant economic or social benefit. Financials forecast for this type of business appear modest in the plan overall. Applicant’s commitment certificate was expired at time of application. Overall, applicant has not adequately demonstrated that he meets all of the requirements of A77. Weighing the factors in this application. I am not satisfied that the applicant will depart Canada at the end of the period authorized for their stay. For the reasons above, I have refused this application

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker's GCMS notes show concerns about financial documents, lack of supporting employment evidence, modest economic benefits, expired certificate, and refusal reasons.

propositions.text: The Officer refused the other Applicants' applications for lack of significant family ties and inconsistent purpose for temporary stay under paragraph 200(1)(b) IRPR.
propositions.quote: The letter issued to each of the other Applicants stated that the Officer was not satisfied the Applicant would leave Canada at the end of their stay as required by paragraph 200(1)(b) of the IRPR, based on: (a) the Applicant not having significant family ties outside Canada; and (b) the purpose of their visit to Canada not being consistent with a temporary stay given the details provided in the application.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker refused the other Applicants' applications due to lack of family ties and inconsistent temporary stay purpose under paragraph 200(1)(b) IRPR.

propositions.text: The Officer's GCMS notes for other Applicants reflect reasons consistent with refusal letters and reference the Principal Applicant's refusal.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s GCMS notes reflect reasons consist with those letters, as well as referencing the fact that the Principal Applicant’s application had been refused.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker's GCMS notes for other Applicants align with refusal letters and reference the Principal Applicant's refusal.

propositions.text: The Court must determine if the Decision is reasonable on its merits and if the Officer deprived the Applicants of procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: Based on the parties’ submissions, which concern the Officer’s reasons for the Decision as it relates to the Principal Applicant, the issues for the Court to determine in this application are: whether the Decision is reasonable on its merits; and whether the Officer deprived the Applicants of procedural fairness in arriving at the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies issues: whether the Decision is reasonable and whether procedural fairness was denied to the Applicants.

propositions.text: The merits of the Decision are reviewable on the reasonableness standard per Supreme Court's Vavilov decision.
propositions.quote: As is implicit in the articulation of the first issue, the merits of the Decision are reviewable on the standard of reasonableness, as informed by the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Decision's merits are reviewed on reasonableness standard per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness requires assessing whether the procedure was fair in all circumstances, per Canadian Pacific Railway v Canada.
propositions.quote: The procedural fairness determination requires the Court to assess whether the procedure followed was fair having regard to all the circumstances (Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54).

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness requires assessing fairness of procedure in all circumstances per Canadian Pacific Railway v Canada.

propositions.text: The court will address reasonableness and procedural fairness together by analyzing the Decision's bases the Applicants challenge.
propositions.quote: Rather than considering the parties’ arguments surrounding reasonableness and procedural fairness as two separate issues, it will be most efficient to structure these Reasons around the various bases for the Decision that the Applicants seek to impugn.

paragraphs.summary: The court will analyze reasonableness and procedural fairness together by examining the Decision's challenged bases.

propositions.text: The Officer's GCMS notes show concern that the Principal Applicant did not provide supporting documentation for stated employment and education.
propositions.quote: The GCMS notes demonstrate that the Officer’s reasons for the Decision include not being satisfied that the Principal Applicant would be able to adequately perform the proposed work. The Officer noted the Applicant’s stated employment and education but found that no supporting documentation had been provided.

propositions.text: At the hearing, the Applicants identified documents in the Principal Applicant’s application addressing employment and education.
propositions.quote: At the hearing of this application, the Applicants identified documents in the Principal Applicant’s work permit application that speak to these subjects.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Officer lacked supporting employment and education documents; Applicants identified such documents at hearing.

propositions.text: Applicants argue the Officer's concern is a veiled credibility finding requiring procedural fairness to notify and allow response.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that the Officer’s conclusion represents a concern with the authenticity of the Principal Applicant’s experience and qualifications and therefore a veiled credibility finding, imposing upon the Officer a procedural fairness obligation to advise the Principal Applicant of that concern and afford him an opportunity to address it before making the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants argue the Officer's concern is a veiled credibility finding triggering procedural fairness obligations.

propositions.text: Respondent accepts credibility concerns increase procedural fairness duties but denies Officer made a credibility finding here.
propositions.quote: The Respondent accepts that credibility concerns heighten the procedural fairness obligations owed to an applicant and give rise to a duty to provide an opportunity to address such concerns. However, the Respondent disagrees with the Applicants’ characterization of the Officer’s concerns with the Principal Applicant’s experience and qualifications as a credibility finding.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent agrees credibility concerns increase fairness duties but denies the Officer made a credibility finding here.

propositions.text: The Officer's concern was about sufficiency of evidence, not credibility; no procedural fairness breach arises from sufficiency concerns.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent’s characterization of the documents upon which the Applicants rely as representing self-descriptions by the Principal Applicant, and I further agree with the Respondent that the Officer’s concern in relation to those documents was with the sufficiency of this evidence. The GCMS notes do not demonstrate the Officer raising a credibility or authenticity concern. Rather, the concern was that the Principal Applicant failed to provide any sort of supporting documentation in relation to his stated employment or education. Visa officers are not required to inform applicants of concerns regarding the sufficiency of supporting materials or evidence (Mohamud v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 1140 [Mohamud] at para 14; Patel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 77 at para 10).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's concern was about evidence sufficiency, not credibility, so no procedural fairness breach occurred.

propositions.text: No procedural fairness breach found regarding the Officer's concern about employment and education evidence.
propositions.quote: I find no breach of procedural fairness in connection with this aspect of the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes no procedural fairness breach occurred regarding employment and education evidence concerns.

propositions.text: The Officer was not satisfied with the Principal Applicant's financial evidence due to outdated bank statements.
propositions.quote: The GCMS notes further demonstrate that the Officer was not satisfied with the evidence provided in support of the Principal Applicant’s financial ability. The Officer states that the funds available at the time of application were unclear, because the bank statements were outdated compared to the date of the application.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker was not satisfied with the Principal Applicant's financial evidence due to outdated bank statements.

propositions.text: Applicants argue the Officer's financial concerns are a veiled credibility finding.
propositions.quote: Again, the Applicants submit that this conclusion represents a veiled credibility finding.

propositions.text: The court disagrees that the Officer's concern about outdated bank statements is a credibility finding; it is about insufficiency of evidence.
propositions.quote: I again disagree with this characterization of the Officer’s reasoning. I appreciate that, unlike the self-descriptions of education and experience canvassed above, the bank statements are documentation generated by a financial institution. However, the Officer’s concern was that the statements were not current and therefore were insufficient to demonstrate the Principal Applicant’s financial capacity.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue financial concerns are veiled credibility findings; the court disagrees, finding concerns about evidence insufficiency.

propositions.text: Applicants argue financial documentation was same as provided by Incubator and correspondence invited IRCC to request updates
propositions.quote: the Applicants note that the financial documentation submitted in support of the Principal Applicant’s application were the same as had been provided by the Incubator, and that the accompanying correspondence from the Principal Applicant’s representative to IRCC stated that, should IRCC require updated documents, it should not hesitate to send a request letter.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant had onus to provide sufficient documentation; Officer had no obligation to inform of concerns about sufficiency
propositions.quote: It was the Principal Applicant’s onus to provide sufficient documentation and, as noted above, the Officer had no obligation to inform the Principal Applicant of concerns as to the sufficiency of his submissions (Mohamud at para 14).

propositions.text: Correspondence to IRCC does not alter principle that onus is on Principal Applicant to provide sufficient documentation
propositions.quote: The correspondence to IRCC does not alter that principle.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue financial documents were same as Incubator's and correspondence invited IRCC to request updates; court finds onus on Principal Applicant to provide sufficient documents and correspondence does not alter this.

propositions.text: Applicants raise concerns about Officer's comments on accountants' documentation implying credibility issues due to paid reports
propositions.quote: The Applicants raise similar concerns with respect to the Officer’s comments on the documentation from the Principal Applicant’s accountants. The GCMS notes state, “These documents will not be considered given that the report(s) are a paid for document/statement and do not include evidence of funds available that are not already been reviewed.” I agree with the Applicants that this statement by the Officer implies a concern about the credibility of the accountants’ documentation, based on the fact that the accountants are paid for their services.

propositions.text: Such concern about credibility could give rise to procedural fairness obligation
propositions.quote: This is the sort of concern that could give rise to a procedural fairness obligation.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Officer's comments imply credibility concerns about paid accountants' reports, which could trigger procedural fairness obligations, court agrees.

propositions.text: Respondent argues failure to alert Principal Applicant to credibility concern is not material because accountants' info dated 2023 and could not cure currency concern
propositions.quote: I accept the Respondent’s position that, in the matter at hand, the failure of the Officer to alert the Principal Applicant to this concern, and afford an opportunity to respond thereto, is not material to the Decision. As the Respondent notes (and consistent with the Officer’s statement), the information from the accountants, like the bank statements, dated to 2023 and therefore did not have the potential to cure the Officer’s concern that the information was not current.

propositions.text: Court accepts Respondent's position that failure to alert is not material to Decision
propositions.quote: I accept the Respondent’s position that, in the matter at hand, the failure of the Officer to alert the Principal Applicant to this concern, and afford an opportunity to respond thereto, is not material to the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues failure to alert Principal Applicant to credibility concern is not material; court accepts this position.

propositions.text: No breach of procedural fairness found
propositions.quote: Again, I find no breach of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no breach of procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Applicants note Officer's GCMS notes state Commitment Certificate expired at application time, which is factually inaccurate
propositions.quote: The Applicants note the statement in the Officer’s GCMS notes that the Commitment Certificate had expired at the time of application.

propositions.text: Respondent accepts factual inaccuracy about Commitment Certificate expiry date
propositions.quote: The Respondent accepts this assertion.

propositions.text: Applicants argue factual error is significant and undermines reasonableness of Decision
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that the Officer’s error represents a significant misapprehension of the facts underlying the application, which undermines the reasonableness of the Decision.

propositions.text: Respondent argues error is not material; sufficiency of evidence on funds and ability to perform work are determinative
propositions.quote: The Respondent takes the position that this error is not material, arguing that the Officer’s principal reasons for refusing the Principal Applicant’s work permit application were the sufficiency of evidence on available funds and the sufficiency of evidence establishing the Principal Applicant’s ability to perform the relevant work.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants note factual error about Commitment Certificate expiry; Respondent accepts error but argues it is not material as other reasons are determinative.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Respondent that factual error about Commitment Certificate is not reviewable error
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent’s position that, on the facts of this case, the factual error with respect to the Commitment Certificate does not represent a reviewable error.

propositions.text: Officer's reasoning on funds and ability to perform work are determinative issues
propositions.quote: I accept the Respondent’s position that the Officer’s reasoning with respect to availability of funds and ability to perform the relevant work are themselves determinative issues.

propositions.text: Factual error does not undermine reasonableness of Decision
propositions.quote: the factual error in relation to the Commitment Certificate does not undermine the reasonableness of the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees factual error about Commitment Certificate is not reviewable and does not undermine reasonableness as other reasons are determinative.

propositions.text: Unclear if Officer considered expiry issue determinative; even if so, other reasons are determinative
propositions.quote: It is not particularly clear from the GCMS notes whether the Officer considered what they misunderstood to be submission of the application after the expiry of the Commitment Certificate to be a determinative issue. However, even if the Decision were to be interpreted in that manner, I accept the Respondent’s position that the Officer’s reasoning with respect to availability of funds and ability to perform the relevant work are themselves determinative issues.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds unclear if Officer considered expiry issue determinative but other reasons remain determinative even if so.

propositions.text: Officer noted financial forecast for salaries under $50,000 for first five years, so no significant economic or social benefits shown
propositions.quote: the Principal Applicant’s financial forecast for salaries was under $50,000 for each of the first five years of business, the Principal Applicant had not satisfied the Officer of the creation of significant economic or social benefits.

propositions.text: Paragraph 205(a) IRPR allows work permit if work creates or maintains significant social, cultural or economic benefits
propositions.quote: paragraph 205(a) of the IRPR, which provides that a work permit may be issued to a foreign national who intends to perform work that would create or maintain significant social, cultural or economic benefits or opportunities for Canadian citizens or permanent residents.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found financial forecast under $50,000 did not show significant benefits; paragraph 205(a) IRPR governs work permits for such benefits.

propositions.text: Applicants note written submissions referenced various economic, social, cultural benefits beyond salaries
propositions.quote: the Applicants noted at the hearing of this application that the written submissions in support of the Principal Applicant’s work permit application referenced a variety of economic benefits, social benefits, and cultural benefits, which extended beyond the impacts of the salaries to be paid to Canadian workers.

propositions.text: Officer's analysis does not reference other categories of benefits
propositions.quote: The Officer’s analysis does not reference these other categories of benefits.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue submissions referenced various benefits beyond salaries; Officer's analysis did not reference these.

propositions.text: Court accepts Applicants' point about other benefits
propositions.quote: I accept this point.

propositions.text: Officer's reasoning on funds and ability to perform work are determinative issues
propositions.quote: the Officer’s reasoning with respect to availability of funds and ability to perform the relevant work are themselves determinative issues.

propositions.text: Shortcoming in benefits analysis does not undermine reasonableness of Decision overall
propositions.quote: any shortcoming in the Officer’s benefits analysis does not undermine the reasonableness of the Decision overall.

paragraphs.summary: Court accepts Applicants' point on benefits but finds shortcomings do not undermine reasonableness as other reasons are determinative.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review dismissed
propositions.quote: this application for judicial review will be dismissed.

propositions.text: No question certified for appeal
propositions.quote: No question is certified for appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review application and certifies no question for appeal.
